---
title: "Geographic analysis"
---

In the previous chapter, we looked at election precincts in Prince George's County to show a bit of a pattern regarding concentration of the precincts with the most and 0 eligible voters. Let's go little further and look at voters statewide.

First, let's load the libraries we'll need, including tigris. We're also going to load tidycensus and set an API key for tidycensus.

```{r}
#| output: false
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(janitor)
library(tigris)
library(tidycensus)
```

If you haven't already stored your Census API key (see the Census chapter), do that now:

```{r}
#| eval: false
census_api_key("YOUR API KEY HERE", install=TRUE)
```

In the previous chapter, we looked at COVID-19 cases by zip codes to find patterns in Maryland. Let's go further and, instead of using raw numbers, use rates based on the population of each county.

For the rest of this chapter, we're going to work on building a map that will help us gain insight into geographic patterns in COVID-19 cases by county in Maryland. What geographic patterns can we identify?

First, we'll load the county COVID-19 case data and get population data for each county using tidycensus. The variable for total population is B01001_001. The case data has one row for each day from March 2020 until the state stopped updating it in 2025, and one column for each county, with the total number of cases reported since the pandemic began. We only want the latest totals, so we'll use `slice_tail()` to keep just the last row, then use `pivot_longer()` to turn the county columns into rows.

```{r}
md_county_cases <- read_csv("data/md_covid_cases_by_county.csv") |> slice_tail(n=1) |> pivot_longer(cols=-c('OBJECTID', 'DATE'), names_to='county', values_to = 'cases')

md_county_population <- get_acs(geography = "county",
              variables = c(population = "B01001_001"),
              year = 2023,
              state = "MD")
```

Ultimately, we're going to join this county table with population with COVID-19 cases by county, and then calculate a rate. But remember, we then want to visualize this data by drawing a county map that helps us pick out trends. Thinking ahead, we know we'll need a county map shapefile. Fortunately, we can pull this geometry information right from tidycensus at the same time that we pull in the population data by adding "geometry = TRUE" to our get_acs function.

```{r}
md_county_population <- get_acs(geography = "county",
              variables = c(population = "B01001_001"),
              year = 2023,
              state = "MD",
              geometry = TRUE)

md_county_population
```

We now have a new column, geometry, that contains the "MULTIPOLYGON" data that will draw an outline of each county when we go to draw a map.

The next step will be to join our population data to our case data on the county column.

But there's a problem. The column in our population data that has county names is called "NAME", and it has the full name of the county with "County" and "Maryland" in it. The case data just has the name of the county, with underscores instead of spaces and no punctuation. For example, the population data has "Prince George's County, Maryland" and the case data has "Prince_Georges".

```{r}
md_county_population

md_county_cases
```

If they're going to join properly, we need to clean one of them up to make it match the other.

Let's clean the population table. We're going to rename the "NAME" column to "county", then use `str_remove_all()` to remove " County, Maryland" or ", Maryland" and any apostrophes or periods, and make the county titlecase (so that "Baltimore city" becomes "Baltimore City"). Next we'll replace the spaces with underscores so the names match the case data exactly. We're also going to rename the column that contains the population information from "estimate" to "population" and select only the county name and the population columns, along with the geometry. That leaves us with this tidy table.

```{r}
md_county_population <- md_county_population |>
  rename(county = NAME) |>
  mutate(county = str_to_title(str_remove_all(county, " County, Maryland|, Maryland|'|\\."))) |>
  mutate(county = str_replace_all(county, " ", "_")) |>
  rename(population = estimate) |>
  select(county, population, geometry)

md_county_population
```

Now we can join them.

```{r}
md_pop_with_cases <- md_county_population |>
  left_join(md_county_cases, join_by(county))

md_pop_with_cases
```

Our final step before visualization, let's calculate the number of cases per 1,000 people and sort from highest to lowest to see what trends we can identify just from the table.

```{r}
md_pop_with_cases <- md_county_population |>
  left_join(md_county_cases, join_by(county)) |> 
  mutate(rate = cases/population*1000) |>
  arrange(desc(rate))

md_pop_with_cases
```

Let's take a look at the result of this table. Allegany County, in far western Maryland, had the highest rate of reported cases -- about 373 for every 1,000 residents -- followed by Dorchester and Garrett counties. Carroll and Calvert counties had the lowest. Keep in mind what this data measures: *reported* cases. Once home tests became common in 2022, many people who tested positive never reported it, so these numbers undercount how many people actually got sick, and the undercount may not be the same everywhere.

First, let's use the counties() function from tigris to pull down a shapefile of all U.S. counties and grab the ones for Maryland.

```{r}

md_counties <- counties() |>
  filter(STATEFP == "24")

```

Okay, now let's visualize. We're going to build a choropleth map, with the color of each county -- the fill -- set according to the number of cases per 1,000 people on a color gradient.

```{r}
county_centroids <- st_centroid(md_counties)
county_centroids_df <- as.data.frame(st_coordinates(county_centroids))
county_centroids_df$NAME <- county_centroids$NAME

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data=md_pop_with_cases, aes(fill=rate)) +
  geom_text(aes(x = X, y = Y, label = NAME), data = county_centroids_df, size = 3, check_overlap = TRUE) +
  theme_minimal()
```

This map is okay, but the color scale makes it hard to draw fine-grained differences. Let's try applying the magma color scale we learned in the last chapter.

```{r}
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data=md_pop_with_cases, aes(fill=rate)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_fill_viridis_b(option="magma")
```

The highest ranking counties stand out nicely in this version, but it's still hard to make out fine-grained differences between other counties.

So let's change the color scale to a "log" scale, which will help us see those differences a bit more clearly.

```{r}
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data=md_pop_with_cases, aes(fill=rate)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_fill_viridis_b(option="magma",trans = "log")
```
